6398-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Grammar was far from fashionable at early Rome, Suetonius says, of little use in a rude society at constant war, with scant time for liberal arts. Its first pretensions were slender. The earliest learned men, poets and orators both, were half Greek: Livius and Ennius, who taught both languages at Rome and abroad, though they mostly translated from Greek. From such beginnings, eminent grammarians rose, and this volume collects their lives.

Cato's house, with marble slabs and gardens worthy of Priapus as guardian, draws a poet's jest. Bibaculus asks how three cabbages and half a pound of meal could nourish wisdom to old age. Suetonius writes scholars as he wrote emperors, through anecdote, quotation, and rivalry, showing how Rome learned to read itself. The volume is a history of language study, from warlike indifference to a discipline with masters and schools.
8466-musa-pedestris-three-centuries-of-c:
John S. Farmer collected three centuries of canting songs and slang rhymes, from 1536 to 1896, in Musa Pedestris. Contents list an index of titles and authors, forewords, notes, and an appendix. They open with a beggar's song from 1660, a Middleton and Dekker piece from 1611, and a Matsell song from 1859, among many others.

Cant is the secret language of thieves, beggars, and the underworld, and Farmer, a lexicographer of slang, annotates each piece. Readers get the underworld's own poetry, from Elizabethan rogues to Victorian music halls, with notes explaining the slang. The volume is a treasure for students of English slang, and a lively, rough anthology for the curious.
musa-pedestris-three-centuries-of-cantin:
John S. Farmer collected and annotated three centuries of canting songs and slang rhymes. The dates run from 1536 to 1896. Cant was the secret slang of beggars, thieves, and street folk. Farmer prints their ballads with notes and indexes of titles and authors.

Songs here come from Dekker, Middleton, Pierce Egan, and many unnamed singers. Titles promise beggars' curses, cadgers' balls, and costers' serenades. Some are coarse, some comic, and all are rich in lost street speech. The book saves the songs of the poor and the rogue. Scholars of slang and song still mine it for early low-life verse.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1:
Beyond the emperors, Suetonius also wrote lives of scholars, and volume thirteen of this set holds his Lives of Eminent Grammarians, in the Thomson translation revised by T. Forester. He opens by noting that grammar was far from fashionable in early Rome. A people busy with constant wars had little time for liberal arts, and the earliest learned men, Livius and Ennius, were half-Greek poets and orators who mostly translated Greek work.

Credit for bringing grammar to Rome goes to Crates of Mallos, an envoy from King Attalus. Between the second and third Punic wars he fell into an open sewer in the Palatine quarter, broke his leg, and spent his recovery giving lectures. Suetonius turns even scholarship into biography, full of accident and character.
